body: Differentiate between the following: (i) **health-related** and **performance (skill)-related** physical fitness (ii) **intellectual** wellness and **environmental** wellness (iii) **drug use** and **drug abuse**.
answer:
**(i)**
| Health-related fitness | Performance (skill)-related fitness |
|---|---|
| Components that **promote health** and reduce disease risk, needed by **everyone** | Components that improve **sports and motor performance** |
| **Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition** | **Agility, balance, coordination, power, speed, reaction time** |

**(ii)**
| Intellectual wellness | Environmental wellness |
|---|---|
| Engaging the mind in **creative, stimulating activities**, lifelong learning, critical thinking, problem-solving | Living in harmony with, and caring for, one's **surroundings**: clean, safe home, school and community; protecting nature |
| e.g. reading, learning new skills, debating | e.g. recycling, sanitation, avoiding pollution |

**(iii)**
| Drug use | Drug abuse |
|---|---|
| Taking a drug **correctly for its intended (medical) purpose**, in the right dose, as prescribed | **Misusing** a drug (illegal drugs, or legal drugs in excess or for non-medical purposes) in a way that **harms** health or functioning |
| e.g. taking paracetamol as directed | e.g. abusing tramadol or codeine syrup, smoking marijuana, binge drinking |

> [!answer]
> Health-related fitness (cardio endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition) is for health; skill-related (agility, balance, coordination, power, speed, reaction time) is for performance. Intellectual wellness = an active, learning mind; environmental wellness = caring for surroundings. Drug use = correct, intended use; drug abuse = harmful misuse.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Health-related components predict **disease risk** (hypokinetic diseases); skill-related components are largely **genetically influenced** and matter for athletes. Wellness is **multidimensional**; intellectual and environmental dimensions interact with physical, emotional, social, spiritual and occupational wellness. Drug abuse among Ghanaian youth (tramadol, 'wee', codeine) is a major concern.

## Simplified explanation

Health fitness keeps you **healthy**; skill fitness helps you **play sports well**. Intellectual wellness = **keeping your mind active**; environmental wellness = **caring for your surroundings**. Using a drug **as directed** is use; using it **wrongly** is abuse.
hint: Define each side, then contrast with examples.

body: Explain the following terms and give **two examples** each: (i) **Distress** (ii) **Eustress**. State any **three** ways of **managing stress**.
answer:
- **Distress:** **negative stress**: stress perceived as harmful or overwhelming, leading to anxiety, poor performance and illness. _Examples:_ death of a loved one, failing an exam, financial problems, divorce, job loss, conflict.
- **Eustress:** **positive stress**: stress perceived as challenging and motivating, enhancing performance. _Examples:_ preparing for a competition, starting a new job, getting married, a promotion, a planned holiday, studying for an exam you feel ready for.

**Managing stress (any three):** **regular physical exercise** · **relaxation techniques** (deep breathing, meditation, prayer, yoga) · **time management** and planning · **adequate sleep** and a healthy diet · **talking to someone** (social support, counselling) · **positive thinking** and realistic goals · hobbies and recreation · avoiding drugs and alcohol.

> [!answer]
> Distress = harmful negative stress (e.g. bereavement, failing exams); eustress = positive, motivating stress (e.g. competing, a new job). Manage stress through exercise, relaxation, time management, sleep and diet, social support, positive thinking, hobbies.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hans Selye distinguished eustress from distress; the **Yerkes–Dodson curve** shows performance rises with arousal up to an optimum, then falls. Whether a stressor is eustress or distress depends on **perception and coping resources** (Lazarus). Exercise reduces stress hormones and releases endorphins.

## Simplified explanation

**Distress** is bad stress (like losing someone); **eustress** is good stress (like preparing for a match). Reduce stress by **exercising, relaxing, planning your time, sleeping well and talking to people**.

body: Mention **three** things that **warm-up** does to the body and **three** things that **cool-down** does to the body. _(Also asked: explain warm-up, workout/activity and cool-down as they apply to an exercise programme.)_
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Warm-up** (5–10 minutes of light activity and dynamic stretching **before** exercise): **raises heart rate** and blood flow to muscles · **increases body and muscle temperature** · **improves muscle elasticity and joint mobility** · **prevents injuries** · prepares the mind (psychological readiness) · improves nerve conduction and reaction.
>
> **Workout/activity:** the **main conditioning phase**, where the planned exercise (aerobic, strength, sport skills) is done at the target intensity and duration.
>
> **Cool-down** (5–10 minutes of light activity and static stretching **after** exercise): **gradually lowers heart rate and breathing** to resting levels · **prevents blood pooling** in the legs (dizziness, fainting) · helps **remove lactic acid**/waste and reduces muscle soreness · lowers body temperature · improves flexibility through stretching.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A complete exercise session has **three phases**: warm-up → workout (conditioning) → cool-down. Skipping the warm-up increases the risk of strains; skipping the cool-down can cause **venous pooling** and post-exercise hypotension.

## Simplified explanation

**Warm-up** gets your heart, muscles and mind ready and prevents injury. **Cool-down** slowly brings your body back to rest and reduces soreness and dizziness.

answer:
> [!answer]
> Any two: **bouncing (ballistic stretching)** without proper training · stretching **cold muscles** (stretch after warming up) · **holding your breath** · **overstretching** to the point of **pain** · locking (hyperextending) the joints · comparing yourself with others and forcing a range of motion.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Static stretches should be held about **15–30 seconds** to the point of mild tension, not pain. Ballistic stretching triggers the **stretch reflex**, increasing injury risk.

## Simplified explanation

Don't **bounce**, don't stretch **cold muscles**, don't **hold your breath**, and don't stretch until it **hurts**.

body: State **three** basic factors to consider when **designing a fitness programme**, and **three** groups of people with **special needs** you must consider.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Factors:** the individual's **current fitness level and health status** (medical screening, PAR-Q) · **goals/objectives** (weight loss, endurance, strength) · **age and sex** · **available time, facilities and equipment** · **principles of training** (FITT, progression, overload) · interests and preferences · safety.
>
> **Special-needs groups:** **persons with disabilities** (physical, visual, hearing) · **pregnant women** · **the elderly/aged** · **children** · people with **chronic conditions** (asthma, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, obesity) · people recovering from injury.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Programmes should be **individualised**: a pre-participation screening (e.g. **PAR-Q+**) identifies people needing medical clearance. Special populations need modified intensity, supervision and adapted activities.

## Simplified explanation

Consider the person's **fitness, health, goals, age, time and equipment**. Take special care with **disabled people, pregnant women, the elderly, children and people with chronic illness**.

body: Explain the following **principles of training**: (i) **overload** (ii) **intensity** (iii) **reversibility**. Why is it important to follow the principles of training when planning a workout?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **(i) Overload:** to improve fitness, the body must be worked **harder than it is used to** (more weight, distance, time or speed), so it adapts.
> **(ii) Intensity:** **how hard** the exercise is: measured by heart rate (e.g. 60–85% of maximum heart rate), weight lifted, or perceived exertion.
> **(iii) Reversibility:** fitness gains are **lost** when training stops or reduces ('use it or lose it'); detraining begins within weeks.
>
> **Why follow the principles:** to ensure **safe, effective and steady improvement** in fitness while **preventing injury and overtraining**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Other principles: **specificity** (train for the specific outcome), **progression** (increase load gradually), **individuality**, **rest and recovery**, **variety**. Overload is applied through the **FITT** variables.

## Simplified explanation

Push **a bit harder** than usual (overload), choose **how hard** to work (intensity), and remember fitness **fades if you stop** (reversibility). Following these keeps training **safe and effective**.
hint: Overload, how hard, use it or lose it.

answer:
> [!answer]
> - **F: Frequency:** **how often** you exercise (e.g. 3–5 days per week).
> - **I: Intensity:** **how hard** you exercise (e.g. 60–85% of maximum heart rate; moderate vs vigorous).
> - **T: Time (duration):** **how long** each session lasts (e.g. 20–60 minutes).
> - **T: Type:** the **kind of activity** (jogging, swimming, weight training, aerobics), which should match the fitness goal.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

To apply **overload** and **progression**, increase one FITT variable at a time (e.g. add 10% more time per week). WHO recommends adults do at least **150–300 minutes of moderate** (or 75–150 vigorous) aerobic activity per week plus muscle strengthening twice a week.

## Simplified explanation

FITT = **how often**, **how hard**, **how long**, and **what type** of exercise.

body: **Scenario:** Ama goes to the gym **4 times a week** and spends **2 hours**. She **jogs on the treadmill for 30 minutes**, **works out with weights for 45 minutes**, then **cools down and stretches for 15 minutes**, and finally stays in the gym cafeteria for about 30 minutes before going home. Indicate the **duration**, **frequency** and **specificity** of Ama's workout.
answer:
> [!answer]
> - **Duration:** **90 minutes** of actual exercise per session (30 + 45 + 15); the 30 minutes in the cafeteria is **not** exercise.
> - **Frequency:** **4 times a week**.
> - **Specificity:** her training targets **cardiorespiratory endurance** (treadmill jogging) and **muscular strength/endurance** (weights), plus **flexibility** (stretching).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This tests applying the FITT and specificity principles to a real schedule. **Specificity** means adaptations match the type of training: jogging improves aerobic fitness, weights improve muscular fitness.

## Simplified explanation

Ama exercises **90 minutes** (not 2 hours: the cafeteria doesn't count), **4 times a week**, training her **heart/lungs** and **muscles**.

body: Mention the **two most essential elements** to consider when planning an **aerobic dance** session. State one **advantage** and one **disadvantage** of exercising in a **group**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Aerobic dance elements:** **music** (its tempo or beats per minute must suit the intensity) and **choreography/movement** (safe, rhythmic steps matched to participants' level), with proper **warm-up and cool-down**.
>
> **Group exercise:** _Advantage:_ **motivation, social support and enjoyment**; people push each other and are more likely to keep going. _Disadvantage:_ **less individual attention**: the pace may not suit everyone (too hard or too easy), increasing injury risk or boredom.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Aerobic dance intensity is controlled by **tempo (BPM)**, impact level (low vs high impact) and arm movements. Group settings boost **adherence** through social facilitation, but programmes should offer **modifications** for different fitness levels.

## Simplified explanation

Aerobic dance needs the right **music** and **moves**. Groups are **fun and motivating** but can't always suit **each person's level**.
hint: Music and movement; motivation vs individualisation.

body: What is the relationship between **nutrition and weight management**? State any three ways of achieving a **healthy body weight** (measures that can help in weight loss).
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Relationship:** body weight depends on **energy balance**: calories taken in through food versus calories used in metabolism and activity. **Good nutrition** (the right amounts and types of food) keeps intake in balance with expenditure; eating more than you burn causes **weight gain**, and less causes **weight loss**.
>
> **Ways to a healthy weight:** **balanced diet** with controlled portions · **regular physical activity** · reduce **sugary drinks, fried and fatty foods** and processed snacks · eat more **fruits, vegetables and whole grains** (fibre) · **drink water** · avoid skipping breakfast and late-night eating · **adequate sleep** and stress control · set realistic goals and monitor weight/BMI.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

About **7,700 kcal ≈ 1 kg** of body fat; a daily deficit of 500 kcal leads to about 0.5 kg loss per week. Healthy BMI: **18.5–24.9 kg/m²**. Sustainable weight management combines diet, activity and behaviour change rather than crash diets.

## Simplified explanation

Weight depends on **food in versus energy used**. To stay healthy, **eat balanced meals, exercise, cut sugar and fat, drink water and sleep well**.

body: Explain any **three** factors that **influence the choice of food** individuals make.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Any three: **culture and religion** (food traditions, taboos, e.g. Muslims avoid pork) · **income/economic status** (affordability) · **availability and season** (local foods, market access) · **taste and personal preference** · **knowledge of nutrition** and health status (diabetics, allergies) · **family and peer influence** · **advertising and media** · **convenience and time** (fast foods) · **age and sex** (life-stage needs).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Food choice is shaped by **biological, economic, physical, social, psychological and cultural** determinants. Nutrition education must work with these factors (e.g. promoting affordable local foods such as beans, kontomire and fish).

## Simplified explanation

People choose food based on **culture, money, what's available, taste, knowledge and friends or advertising**.
hint: Why do we eat what we eat?

body: Differentiate between **good nutrition** and **poor nutrition**, and between a **bounce pass** and a **chest pass** in basketball.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Good nutrition:** eating a **balanced diet** with the right amounts of all nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water) for growth, energy and health. **Poor nutrition (malnutrition):** an **inadequate, excessive or unbalanced** intake, leading to **undernutrition** (kwashiorkor, stunting, anaemia) or **overnutrition** (obesity, diabetes).
>
> **Chest pass:** the ball is thrown with two hands from the **chest directly through the air** to a teammate's chest: fast and accurate over short to medium distances. **Bounce pass:** the ball is pushed so it **bounces once on the floor** (about two-thirds of the way) before reaching the teammate, which is useful to get **past a defender's arms**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Malnutrition includes **both** under- and over-nutrition (the 'double burden' seen in Ghana). In basketball, passing choice depends on defender position: bounce passes are harder to intercept but slower.

## Simplified explanation

Good nutrition = **balanced** food; poor nutrition = **too little, too much or the wrong** food. A chest pass goes **straight through the air**; a bounce pass **hits the floor once**.

body: Mention **two exercises** each that can be used to develop: (i) **agility** (ii) **power** (iii) **muscular endurance** (iv) **muscular strength**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> | Component | Exercises |
> |---|---|
> | **Agility** | Shuttle runs, zig-zag/cone drills, ladder drills, side-steps, dodging games |
> | **Power** | Plyometrics (box jumps, bounding), vertical/broad jumps, medicine-ball throws, sprint starts |
> | **Muscular endurance** | Push-ups, sit-ups/crunches, planks, squats with high repetitions, circuit training |
> | **Muscular strength** | Weight lifting (bench press, squats, deadlifts) with heavy loads and low reps, pull-ups, resistance-band work |
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Specificity:** strength needs **heavy load, low reps** (e.g. 3–6 reps); endurance needs **light load, high reps** (15+); power combines **force and speed** (explosive movements); agility needs **rapid changes of direction**.

## Simplified explanation

Agility: **shuttle runs**; power: **jumping**; muscular endurance: **many push-ups/sit-ups**; strength: **lifting heavy weights**.
hint: Match the exercise to the component.

body: (a) Explain **five safety measures** to follow before beginning a physical fitness programme. (b) Mention **five categories of people** who are at high risk of **high blood pressure**.
answer:
**(a) Safety measures:**
1. **Medical screening/check-up:** complete a health questionnaire (PAR-Q) or see a doctor, especially if over 40 or with chronic conditions.
2. **Assess current fitness** and set realistic goals; start slowly and **progress gradually**.
3. **Warm up before and cool down after** each session.
4. **Appropriate clothing and footwear** for the activity and weather.
5. **Hydration:** drink water before, during and after exercise; avoid exercising in extreme heat.
6. **Safe environment and equipment:** check facilities and equipment; use proper technique and supervision.
7. **Listen to your body:** stop if you have chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness.

**(b) High-risk groups for hypertension:** **older adults** (over 40/60) · people with a **family history** of hypertension · **obese/overweight** people · **physically inactive** people · those with a **high-salt, high-fat diet** · **heavy alcohol** drinkers and **smokers** · people with **diabetes or kidney disease** · people under chronic **stress** · **pregnant women** (pre-eclampsia) · people of **African descent**.

> [!answer]
> Safety: medical screening, start gradually, warm-up/cool-down, proper attire, hydration, safe equipment and technique, heed warning signs. At risk of hypertension: older adults, family history, obese, inactive, high-salt diet, heavy drinkers and smokers, diabetics and kidney patients, the stressed, pregnant women.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hypertension (≥ 140/90 mmHg) is a leading cause of stroke and heart disease in Ghana. Regular **aerobic exercise** lowers blood pressure by about 5–8 mmHg, but people with uncontrolled hypertension need **medical clearance** and should avoid heavy straining (Valsalva) during lifting.

## Simplified explanation

Before exercising: **get checked**, **start slowly**, **warm up**, **wear the right gear**, **drink water**. Hypertension risk is high in **older, overweight, inactive, salty-food-eating, smoking or drinking** people and those with a **family history**.
hint: Before you start: check health, plan gradually, prepare.

body: (a) What is **wellness**? (b) Explain any **four components of wellness**.
answer:
**(a)** **Wellness** is an **active process of making choices** towards a healthy and fulfilling life: a state of **optimal well-being** across physical, mental, social and other dimensions, beyond the mere absence of disease.

**(b) Components (dimensions):**
1. **Physical wellness:** regular exercise, good nutrition, adequate sleep, avoiding harmful substances, and medical care.
2. **Emotional wellness:** understanding and managing feelings, coping with stress, positive self-esteem.
3. **Intellectual wellness:** lifelong learning, creativity, critical thinking.
4. **Social wellness:** healthy relationships, communication, contributing to the community.
5. **Spiritual wellness:** purpose, meaning, values and beliefs (religious or otherwise).
6. **Environmental wellness:** a clean, safe environment and respect for nature.
7. **Occupational wellness:** satisfaction and balance in work or studies.

> [!answer]
> Wellness = an active process toward optimal, multidimensional well-being. Components: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, spiritual, environmental, occupational.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The wellness model (Hettler's six dimensions; others list seven or eight, including financial) emphasises **personal responsibility** and the **interaction** of dimensions: poor emotional wellness can affect physical health and vice versa. This differs from the WHO definition of health only in its emphasis on **active pursuit**.

## Simplified explanation

Wellness means being **well in every part of life**: body, feelings, mind, relationships, spirit, environment and work.
hint: Wellness is more than not being sick.

body: (a) What is **physical fitness**? (b) Explain any **four principles** of training programmes. (c) Design a **five-station circuit** training for children aged **10–12 years**.
answer:
**(a)** **Physical fitness** is the ability to **carry out daily tasks with vigour and alertness, without undue fatigue**, with enough energy left for leisure and emergencies. It comprises health-related and skill-related components.

**(b) Principles of training:**
1. **Overload:** work harder than usual to stimulate adaptation.
2. **Progression:** increase the workload **gradually** over time.
3. **Specificity:** train the specific component or skill you want to improve.
4. **Reversibility:** gains are lost when training stops.
5. **Individuality:** programmes should suit each person's age, fitness and needs.
6. **Rest and recovery:** allow time for the body to adapt and avoid overtraining.

**(c) Five-station circuit for 10–12-year-olds** (about 30 seconds work, 30 seconds rest, 2 rounds, after a warm-up):
| Station | Activity | Component |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Jumping jacks** | Cardiorespiratory endurance |
| 2 | **Wall push-ups / knee push-ups** | Upper-body muscular endurance |
| 3 | **Cone shuttle run / zig-zag** | Agility, speed |
| 4 | **Bodyweight squats** | Leg strength and endurance |
| 5 | **Skipping (rope)** or **sit-ups/plank** | Coordination / core endurance |

_Safety: age-appropriate bodyweight exercises (no heavy weights), fun format, supervision, water breaks, cool-down._

> [!answer]
> Fitness = carrying out daily tasks vigorously without undue fatigue. Principles: overload, progression, specificity, reversibility, individuality, rest. Circuit: jumping jacks, wall/knee push-ups, shuttle run, squats, skipping or plank: short work bouts, rest, fun and supervised.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Children should do at least **60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily** (WHO), with muscle- and bone-strengthening activities 3 days a week. Circuits suit groups because they are **varied, time-efficient and adaptable**; for this age, emphasise **skill and enjoyment** over load.

## Simplified explanation

Physical fitness = having **energy for daily life**. Train by gradually **working harder**, training what you need, and resting. A kids' circuit: **jumping jacks, wall push-ups, shuttle runs, squats and skipping**.
hint: Design for children: bodyweight, fun, short intervals.

body: (a) What is a **hypokinetic disease**? (b) List any **five** hypokinetic diseases. (c) State **two ways** each to manage or reduce the risk of **four** of the diseases mentioned.
answer:
**(a)** A **hypokinetic disease** is a disease or condition **associated with (caused or worsened by) lack of physical activity** and sedentary living ('hypo' = too little, 'kinetic' = movement).

**(b) Examples:** **coronary heart disease** · **hypertension** · **obesity** · **type 2 diabetes** · **osteoporosis** · **low back pain** · **stroke** · some **cancers** (colon, breast) · depression/anxiety.

**(c) Reducing the risk:**
| Disease | Ways to manage or reduce risk |
|---|---|
| **Coronary heart disease** | Regular aerobic exercise; a low saturated-fat, high-fibre diet; stop smoking; control cholesterol |
| **Hypertension** | Reduce **salt** intake; exercise regularly; maintain healthy weight; limit alcohol; manage stress |
| **Obesity** | Balanced, portion-controlled diet; daily physical activity; limit sugary drinks and fast food |
| **Type 2 diabetes** | Exercise regularly (improves insulin sensitivity); healthy weight; reduce refined sugars and carbohydrates |
| **Osteoporosis** | **Weight-bearing exercise** (walking, jogging, skipping); adequate **calcium and vitamin D** |
| **Low back pain** | Strengthen **core and back muscles**; good **posture** and lifting technique; flexibility exercises |

> [!answer]
> Hypokinetic disease = a condition linked to physical inactivity; e.g. heart disease, hypertension, obesity, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, low back pain; reduce risk with exercise plus disease-specific diet and lifestyle measures.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Physical inactivity is a leading global risk factor for mortality (WHO). Exercise improves blood lipids, blood pressure, insulin sensitivity, bone density and mental health, explaining its protective effect against the whole cluster of hypokinetic diseases.

## Simplified explanation

These are diseases from **not moving enough**: heart disease, high blood pressure, obesity, diabetes, weak bones, back pain. Prevent them with **exercise, healthy food, less salt and sugar, and good posture**.
